question: What is the main job of sensory input in our nervous system?

options.A: Sending commands directly to the skeletal muscles
options.B: Detecting changes inside and outside the body
options.C: Producing hormones to regulate blood pressure
options.D: Processing complex thoughts in the spinal cord

explanation: Think of sensory input as your body's early warning system. Receptors pick up information from both your external environment and your insides so you can react! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h1)

question: When a nurse checks your reflexes and muscle movement, which part of the nervous system's job is being tested?
explanation: You got this! Testing reflexes and muscle movement checks how well the nervous system sends signals out to effectors like muscles to create movement. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h1)

question: Which cells in our nervous tissue are the main ones responsible for passing along electrical signals?
explanation: Neurons are the star players! They are specially built to generate and send electrical impulses all over your body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h2)

question: Why do most primary brain tumors start in neuroglial cells rather than mature neurons?

options.A: Neurons lack a cell membrane to protect against damage
options.B: Glial cells do not require oxygen or glucose supply
options.C: Neurons are too small to undergo cancerous mutations
options.D: Glial cells retain the ability to divide throughout life

explanation: Mature neurons stop dividing once we grow up, but glial cells can keep dividing. Because they keep multiplying, they are much more prone to forming tumors if things go wrong. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which part of a neuron usually acts like the antenna, receiving incoming signals?
explanation: Dendrites are the branch-like structures that reach out to catch signals from neighboring neurons and pass them toward the cell body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h3)

question: What do we call a neuron that has one main axon and many dendrites branching out?
explanation: Since it has multiple extensions (one axon plus many dendrites), it's called a multipolar neuron. These are the most common type in our nervous system! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which helpful cell in the central nervous system acts like a little garbage collector, clearing away germs and dead tissue?
explanation: Microglia are the immune defenders of the central nervous system. They clean up debris and fight off any unwanted invaders. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h4)

question: A patient has an issue with making and circulating cerebrospinal fluid in the brain. Which cells are directly involved?
explanation: Ependymal cells line the brain's ventricles and use tiny hair-like cilia to help produce and keep cerebrospinal fluid flowing smoothly. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h4)

question: What do we call the tiny gaps found between the insulated segments of myelin along an axon?
explanation: The nodes of Ranvier are the bare spots between myelin wraps where electrical signals get a quick boost to travel faster. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h5)

question: How does the myelin coating affect the speed of an electrical signal traveling down a nerve fiber?

options.A: It increases impulse speed via saltatory conduction
options.B: It has no effect on nerve conduction velocity
options.C: It stops the impulse entirely until it reaches a synapse
options.D: It slows impulse speed by creating resistance

explanation: Myelin acts like insulation on an electrical wire. It lets the signal jump rapidly from one node to the next, speeding things up tremendously! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which ion movement mainly causes depolarization when an action potential fires?

options.B: Potassium ions rushing out of the cell
options.C: Chloride ions moving into the axon
options.D: Sodium ions rushing into the cell

explanation: When an action potential starts, sodium channels open wide, letting positive sodium ions flood inside and make the inside of the cell more positive (depolarization). [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h6)

question: Why is the inside of a resting neuron negatively charged compared to the outside?

options.A: The sodium-potassium pump exports more positive ions than it imports
options.B: Potassium ions are actively trapped outside the cell membrane
options.C: Negatively charged proteins are constantly pumped out of the soma
options.D: Chloride channels remain permanently open along the axon

explanation: The sodium-potassium pump is like a hardworking bouncer—it kicks out 3 positive sodium ions for every 2 positive potassium ions it lets in, leaving the inside with a net negative charge. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h6)

question: What triggers neurotransmitter packets to open and release their chemicals into the synaptic cleft?

options.A: Inflow of calcium ions into the axon terminal
options.B: Activation of potassium pumps along the dendrite
options.C: Breakdown of myelin around the terminal bulb
options.D: Direct contact between two adjacent cell membranes

explanation: When the electrical signal reaches the end of the axon, it opens calcium channels. The rushing calcium triggers the vesicles to release their chemical messengers. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of enzymes or reuptake pumps at a chemical synapse?

options.A: To physically connect the presynaptic and postsynaptic cells
options.B: To generate new action potentials directly inside the cleft
options.C: To manufacture extra calcium ions for the next signal
options.D: To clear out neurotransmitters and stop continuous stimulation

explanation: Clearing out used neurotransmitters quickly ensures the receiving cell doesn't keep firing endlessly. It keeps our nervous system precise and controlled! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why central nervous system neurons struggle to repair themselves?

options.A: Schwann cells create perfect guiding tubes for repair
options.B: Oligodendrocytes fail to form functional repair tracts
options.D: Astrocytes form physical scar tissue blocks

explanation: Schwann cells actually help nerves heal, but they live in the *peripheral* nervous system, not the central nervous system. The CNS lacks this helpful environment! [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h8)

question: A patient cuts their forearm badly, damaging a major peripheral nerve, but months later sensation and movement return. What structure made this recovery possible?

options.C: Astrocytes migrating out of the spinal cord
options.D: Schwann cells forming a regeneration tube

explanation: In the peripheral nervous system, surviving Schwann cells rally together to form a pathway or 'tube' that guides the regrowing nerve back to where it belongs. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T6#GNS211_U3_T6_h8)
